Lakshmana's Fury; Tara Pacifies Him

Stories from the Ramayana

Lakshmana's Fury; Tara Pacifies Him

When a Promise Was Forgotten

Everyday telling — Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 29–39

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read it slowly, as if you were sitting at home among everyone, telling it to them.

The yellow boxes hold the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Rama quiet and sorrowful, Lakshmana sharp and full of anger, Hanuman humble, Tara calm and wise, Sugriva afraid and then humble.

(The purple cues) tell you when to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

At the end of every part is a green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listener speak.

The main story of this book is from Valmiki's Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 29–39. Sugriva's coronation and the waiting out of the rains are in the book before this one. Anything else you may want to know about the story is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — the young prince of Ayodhya. Tall, calm, kind. Warm dark brown skin, black hair tied back, simple gold ornaments, a bow in his hand. He sits on Prasravana hill, waiting for news of Sita.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother. Like Rama, but a little shorter and slightly lighter. Bow in hand, a simple green-and-beige forest dress. In this book it is his anger that moves the story forward.

Sugriva — king of the vanaras. Warm brown fur, a long tail, royal robes, a simple gold crown. He has just become king by defeating Vali — and he has sunk into pleasure and forgotten his promise.

Tara — queen of the vanaras, Vali's widow, now Sugriva's wife, Angada's mother. Calm, wise, patient — the heroine of this book. Her wisdom is what saves the day.

Hanuman — Sugriva's minister, son of Vayu the wind. A powerful vanara, light golden-brown fur, a long tail, a gentle and devoted face, a saffron dhoti. He is the first to remind Sugriva of his duty.

Angada — son of Vali and Tara, the young vanara prince, now the crown prince. He carries messages between Lakshmana and Sugriva.

Nila — commander of the vanara army. Sugriva orders him to summon all the vanaras.

Plaksha and Prabhava — two of Sugriva's ministers, who reason with the king when Lakshmana arrives.

1 · Waiting on Prasravana · · WAITING ON PRASRAVANA

The rains were over. Rama and Lakshmana sat on Prasravana hill — and the sky had cleared. The clouds had scattered, the sarasa cranes were flying, and the moonlit nights had grown clear and cool.

Autumn had come — the saptacchada trees were covered in flowers, the bees hummed, and the elephants played. It was the season for travel.

But no news had come from Kishkindha. Sugriva had promised — when the rains were over, the search for Sita would begin. But no messenger had come, no word had arrived.

Rama grieved for Sita. He said to Lakshmana — (slowly, in a voice full of sorrow) “Lakshmana, autumn has come, but Sugriva has not remembered me. He is sunk in pleasure. Go, go to Kishkindha, and give him my message.”

Rama said: “Lakshmana, tell Sugriva — the path by which Vali departed has not yet closed. Honour your promise, or you will have to walk that same path. Vali was killed alone — this time he would not be alone; his kith and kin would go with him.”

Rama's message was harsh — but in his heart there was more sorrow than anger. He knew how great a help Sugriva had been to him — but a promise is a promise.

Pause and think — Rama sent Lakshmana with a harsh message — but was Rama angry, or sorrowful? When someone forgets their promise, should you remind them first, or threaten them at once? And why did Rama send Lakshmana — why did he not go himself?

2 · Hanuman Reminds Him · · HANUMAN REMINDS HIM

In Kishkindha, Sugriva was sunk in pleasure. He had a kingdom, he had a queen, and forgetting years of sorrow, he spent his days and nights in enjoyment. The work of the kingdom was in the ministers' hands — and Sugriva's mind was elsewhere.

But Hanuman was watching. He was Sugriva's minister — and the work of a good minister is to remind the king of the right thing at the right time.

One day Hanuman saw — the sky is clear, the clouds and lightning are gone, the cranes are flying, the moonlight is bright. Autumn has come. And Sugriva is still sunk in pleasure.

Hanuman went to Sugriva — and spoke in sweet, reasonable, helpful words. (in a calm, respectful voice)

Hanuman said: “Maharaja, Rama's work is waiting. The search for Sita is Rama's work — do it. Rama did a great thing for you — he killed Vali without caring for his own life. Now your work is to find his wife, whether she is on the earth or in the sky, and bring her back.”

Hanuman said more — “Rama is wise, he works at the right time. That he is not reminding you does not mean the time has not passed. The moment he reminds you, understand that it is already late.”

And he added — “Rama could, if he wished, bring even the gods, the asuras and the great nagas under his arrows. But he is waiting for you — because he has trusted you.”

Sugriva heard Hanuman's words — and his mind woke up. He called the commander Nila and ordered — “Summon all the vanara commanders. Within fifteen nights everyone must be here — whoever comes late will be put to death.”

Having given the order, Sugriva went back inside his palace — drawn again toward pleasure. He had summoned the vanaras — but he did not go to Rama to tell him that the preparations for the search had begun.

Pause and think — Hanuman did not scold Sugriva — he reminded him in sweet and reasoned words. Is that how someone should be reminded of their duty — by scolding, or by explaining? And Sugriva gave the order — but still did not go to Rama. Is doing the work enough, or is it also a duty to tell the person for whom the work is done?

3 · Lakshmana's Fury · · LAKSHMANA'S FURY

On Prasravana, Rama sat sorrowful — and Lakshmana saw it, and his heart filled with anger.

Lakshmana said: “Brother, this vanara does not walk the path of dharma. He has forgotten your favour. I will go now and kill the false Sugriva — and then, with Angada, all the vanaras will search for Sita.”

Lakshmana's anger was so great that his lips trembled, his eyes turned red, and he took up his bow and set out for Kishkindha.

Rama stopped him. (calmly, but firmly)

Rama said: “Lakshmana, no. One who conquers his anger is the best among men. A good man like you should not do such a wrong. Sugriva helped us before — he offered us his friendship. Remember that. Leave harsh words aside, and remind him of the time with gentle words.”

Lakshmana obeyed his brother — but his anger did not cool. He took his bow and arrows and set out for Kishkindha — and on the way his anger fell on the trees. He broke the branches of sala, tala and ashvakarna trees, and crushed boulders to powder under his feet.

The vanaras of Kishkindha saw Lakshmana coming — eyes red, bow drawn, hissing like a snake in anger — and they grew afraid. They began to cry “kil-kil” — as if trying to please Lakshmana.

Pause and think — Lakshmana said — I will kill Sugriva. Rama said — one who conquers anger is best. Was Lakshmana wrong — or was his anger right, but his way wrong? And Rama sent Lakshmana to Kishkindha — did he know that Lakshmana's anger itself would wake Sugriva up?

4 · At Kishkindha's Gate · · AT KISHKINDHA'S GATE

Lakshmana reached Kishkindha — and saw the beauty of the city. Golden palaces, flowering trees, and on the main road the great houses of the vanara chiefs — Angada's, Mainda's and Dvivida's, Gavaya's and Gavaksha's, Jambavan's, Hanuman's.

But Lakshmana's heart was full of anger — and hearing the jingling of women's ornaments from inside the palace, his anger grew more. He did not go inside — he stood at the gate and drew the bowstring and let it go with force.

The twang of the bow echoed in all directions — as if the sky had split open.

Angada came to Lakshmana, trembling. Lakshmana said — “Go, tell Sugriva that Lakshmana, Rama's younger brother, has come. He is waiting at the gate.”

Lakshmana said: “Angada, tell Sugriva — Rama's brother, who is burning with his brother's sorrow, has come to meet you. He stands at the gate. If you think it right, do his work.”

Angada touched the feet of Sugriva, then the feet of his mother Tara, then the feet of his aunt Ruma — and gave the message. But Sugriva did not hear it at all — he was sunk in wine and love, he had no awareness of anything.

Then two of Sugriva's ministers — Plaksha and Prabhava, who were allowed to enter the women's quarters — went inside with Angada and reasoned with Sugriva.

The ministers said: “Maharaja, Lakshmana has come — he is the one who drives Rama's work forward like a chariot. He stands at the gate. Go quickly, bow your head before him, and calm his anger. Do what Rama has said — stand by your promise.”

The “kil-kil” cries of the vanaras and the ministers' words woke Sugriva — his eyes were red with wine, his ornaments scattered. He grew afraid — Lakshmana was at the gate, and he could not understand what the anger was about. He thought he had already summoned the vanaras.

Pause and think — Sugriva had summoned the vanaras — but he had not told Rama. Is doing the work enough — or is it also necessary to tell the person for whom it was done? And Angada first touched the feet of his elders, and only then gave the message — does respect for elders come before a difficult message?

5 · Tara Comes Out · · TARA COMES OUT

Sugriva was afraid. Lakshmana's anger had reached his ears — and he knew that Lakshmana was Rama's brother, and that Rama was the one who had given him his kingdom.

Sugriva said to Tara — (in a frightened, pleading voice) “Tara, you go. Lakshmana is gentle by nature — but right now he is angry. Your sweet words will calm his mind — then I will meet him.”

Tara came — the queen of the vanaras, calm and patient. When Lakshmana saw her, he stepped aside — in the presence of a woman his anger lessened, and he bowed his head.

Tara asked: “Prince, what is the cause of your anger? Who is not obeying your command? Who is it that walks toward a forest fire?”

Lakshmana answered — “Your husband Sugriva, sunk in pleasure, has forgotten Rama's promise. Rama is burning with sorrow — and Sugriva has not remembered him.”

Tara heard Lakshmana's words — and she was not afraid. She answered with a calm mind.

Tara said — “Lakshmana, first know this: Sugriva has summoned the vanaras. The armies are coming from all directions — they are arriving even now. Your anger is right — but the one you are angry with is already doing the work.”

And Tara invited Lakshmana inside — “Come, come within. Meet Sugriva — and then go to Rama.”

Pause and think — Sugriva sent Tara — because he knew Lakshmana would not rage before a woman. Was that cleverness — or cowardice? And Tara's first question to Lakshmana was — “What is the cause of your anger?” When someone comes in anger, should that be the first question?

6 · Tara's Words · · TARA'S WORDS

Lakshmana went inside — and saw Sugriva. Sugriva stood there, hands folded, head bowed, his eyes red, trembling with fear. Ruma was with him — and Tara too.

Lakshmana spoke in anger —

Lakshmana said: “Sugriva, Brahma spoke a shloka — one who forgets a friend's favour is blameworthy in all the worlds. You have forgotten Rama's favour. Stand by your time, Sugriva — do not walk Vali's path.”

Hearing Lakshmana's words, Sugriva's heart trembled — but before he could speak, Tara spoke. And her words are the heart of this story.

Tara said — “Lakshmana, do not speak such harsh words to Sugriva in particular. He is not worthy of hearing harsh words from your mouth.”

Tara said: “Lakshmana, Sugriva is neither ungrateful, nor a cheat, nor a liar, nor crooked. He knows that through Rama he gained his kingdom, Ruma, and me. How could he forget all that?”

Tara went on — “Sugriva is weary, and still not satisfied with pleasure. Pardon his work — he is caught up in the dharma of his body.”

And then Tara said the thing that only she could say — “Lakshmana, killing Ravana will not be easy. Vali himself told me that Ravana is a great king, with countless rakshasas. Sugriva does not have to do this work alone — he needs your help.”

Tara said too — “Sugriva has summoned all the vanara commanders. They are coming — you will see for yourself. Give up your anger, you who know dharma — be calm.”

There was neither fear nor flattery in Tara's words — only truth. She did not hide Sugriva's fault — but she told the whole truth about him too. And Lakshmana's anger slowly began to cool.

Pause and think — Tara defended Sugriva — but not by lying. She accepted his fault, and she also told the truth about him. Should someone be defended like that — not by hiding the fault, but by telling the whole truth? And Tara told them of Ravana's strength — is it also wisdom to know the strength of one's enemy?

7 · Sugriva Apologises · · SUGRIVA APOLOGISES

After Tara's words, Sugriva stepped forward. He stood before Lakshmana with folded hands and bowed head — and spoke.

Sugriva said: “Lakshmana, I made a mistake. Sunk in pleasure, I forgot my promise. But I have summoned the vanaras — they are coming. Rama's work is my work — I will complete it. Forgive me.”

Lakshmana looked at Sugriva — afraid, humble, hands folded. His anger was now completely gone. And then Lakshmana did what a good man does — he too asked for forgiveness.

Lakshmana said: “Sugriva, forgive me too. I spoke harsh words in anger — they were not fit to be spoken. You are Rama's friend — and one should not speak to a friend like that.”

Both forgave each other — and the crisis passed. Tara's wisdom had done what neither anger nor fear could do.

Then Sugriva said — “Come, let us go to Rama. I will tell him myself that the preparations for the search are made.”

Pause and think — Lakshmana too asked for forgiveness — although he was right. Should one ask forgiveness even when one is right? And Sugriva accepted his mistake — is accepting a mistake a weakness, or a strength?

8 · To Rama · · TO RAMA

Sugriva rode in a palanquin — with Nila, Angada, Hanuman and Lakshmana beside him. On Prasravana hill Rama sat — sorrowful, waiting.

Sugriva stepped down from the palanquin and stood before Rama with folded hands. He said — “Rama, I made a mistake. But I have summoned the vanara armies — they are coming from all directions. Now you tell me — what must we do?”

Rama looked at Sugriva — and his sorrow eased a little. His friend had come — late, but he had come.

Rama said to Sugriva — “Sugriva, now begin the search. To know where Sita is — that is our work.”

Pause and think — Sugriva came late — but he came. Is coming late better than not coming at all? And Rama did not scold Sugriva — he spoke straight about the work. Once you have forgiven someone, should the old matter be left behind?

9 · The Army Gathers · · THE ARMY GATHERS

Within a few days, Kishkindha filled with vanaras. Vanara armies came from every direction — crores of vanaras, from mountains, forests and rivers. They came with their commanders — Nila, Nala, Gaja, Gavaya, Gavaksha, Sharabha, Mainda, Dvivida, Sushena, Jambavan, Dadhimukha, and many more.

Sugriva said to Rama — “Rama, the army has come. Now you tell me — what is our work?”

Rama said — “First we must know whether Sita is alive or not — and where Ravana lives. That is our work.”

Rama said: “Sugriva, this work is yours. You take charge of it — I trust you.”

Sugriva gladly took that responsibility. He formed parties for the search in all four directions — and told each party where it must search.

And so the story that began with Lakshmana's anger came to rest on the preparations for the search. The next day the vanaras would go out in all four directions — and the story of the party that went south would be the greatest of all.

Pause and think — Rama handed the work of the search to Sugriva — he did not do it himself. Is a leader's work to do everything himself — or to hand it to the right person? And Sugriva sent parties in all four directions — would it not have been better to send everyone in one direction?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

In this story a promise was forgotten, anger flared, and one calm voice saved everything.

Sugriva forgot his promise — but he was not a bad man. Hanuman reminded him — but not by scolding. Lakshmana grew angry — but Rama stopped him. And Tara calmed everyone — by speaking the truth.

Ask your listeners:

1. Sugriva had given the order — but he had not told Rama. Is doing the work enough, or is it also a duty to tell the person for whom it was done?

2. Hanuman reminded Sugriva in sweet words. Is that how someone should be reminded of their duty?

3. Rama said — one who conquers anger is best. Is conquering anger easy — or is speaking rightly while angry?

4. Tara defended Sugriva — but not by lying, by telling the whole truth. Should someone be defended like that?

5. Lakshmana was right — yet he asked for forgiveness. Should one ask forgiveness even when one is right?

6. Sugriva accepted his mistake. Is accepting a mistake a weakness, or a strength?

7. Rama handed the work of the search to Sugriva. Is a leader's work to do everything himself — or to hand it to the right person?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

The Main Source

The main story of this book is from Valmiki's Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, sargas 29–39 — Hanuman's reminder, Lakshmana's anger, Tara's pacifying, Sugriva's apology, and the gathering of the army.

Hanuman's Reminder — Sarga 29

Hanuman reminding Sugriva of his duty, Rama's waiting, the order to Nila to summon all the vanaras within fifteen days, and Sugriva's return to his palace — this is the story of sarga 29.

Autumn and Rama's Message — Sarga 30

The passing of the rains, the coming of autumn, Rama's sorrow at separation from Sita, and his sending Lakshmana to Kishkindha — “Vali's path has not yet closed” — this is in sarga 30.

Lakshmana's Anger — Sarga 31

Lakshmana speaking of killing Sugriva, Rama stopping him — “one who conquers anger is best” — Lakshmana's march to Kishkindha, breaking trees and boulders, and Angada carrying the message — this is in sarga 31.

Sugriva Not Hearing — Sargas 31–32

Sugriva remaining sunk in wine and love, the “kil-kil” cries of the vanaras, the ministers Plaksha and Prabhava reasoning with Sugriva, and Sugriva sending Tara — this is the story of sargas 31–32.

Tara's Coming — Sarga 33

Tara meeting Lakshmana, her question — “What is the cause of your anger?” — Lakshmana's answer, and Tara's invitation to come inside — this is in sarga 33.

A Note on Tara's Words

In the traditional text of sarga 33 there are 66 shlokas, but in the critical edition verses 25–62 are not found — commentators treat them as later additions. Those verses contain a long discussion of a king's faults. In this book Tara's reasoning is told as the traditional text gives it — and that fact is stated here separately.

Lakshmana's Rebuke and Tara's Answer — Sargas 34–35

Lakshmana telling Sugriva Brahma's shloka and warning him of Vali's path, and Tara's answer — Sugriva is neither ungrateful, nor a cheat, nor a liar; through Rama he gained his kingdom, Ruma and Tara; the vanara armies have been summoned; and Ravana is mighty, as Vali himself said — this is in sargas 34–35.

Forgiveness and Going to Rama — Sarga 36

Sugriva's apology, Lakshmana asking pardon for his harsh words, and the journey in a palanquin to Rama on Prasravana — this is the story of sarga 36.

The Gathering of the Army — Sargas 37–39

The vanara armies coming in crores, Sugriva asking Rama what the work is, and Rama telling him — to know whether Sita is alive, and to find Ravana's abode — this is in sargas 37–39.

What Happens Next

Parties will go out to search in all four directions — east, west, north and south. The story of the party that went south is in the next books of this series.

The End · · THE END

Here the story of Lakshmana's anger and Tara's pacifying comes to rest — a forgotten promise, a flaring anger, and one calm voice that saved everything.

And whenever it seems to you that someone has forgotten a promise, remember Hanuman — who reminded him in sweet words. And whenever anger comes, remember Tara — who calmed anger by speaking the truth.

— The End —
